entries.title: Scratch
entries.what: Doug Pray's American documentary on turntablism, running from Grandmaster Flash and Grand Wizzard Theodore to the Invisibl Skratch Piklz and Mix Master Mike
entries.why: DJ Q-Bert appears throughout as himself, demonstrating the scratch technique the album and film are built from; released the same year and the straight documentary account of the culture Wave Twisters animates. Grade and tone diverge: the connection is as direct as it gets, but Scratch is a talking-head documentary that explains everything, where Wave Twisters explains nothing.

entries.title: Battle Sounds
entries.what: John Carluccio's 60-minute documentary on competitive DJ battling, shot through the mid-90s and the first film to treat turntablism as its own discipline
entries.why: Q-Bert is a featured DJ alongside Grand Wizard Theodore, Mix Master Mike and Rob Swift; this is the documentary record of the battle circuit Q-Bert dominated and whose techniques the Wave Twisters album is a showcase for. Grade and tone diverge: essential background, but it is handheld vérité footage of people talking about records, not a cartoon.

entries.title: Hang the DJ
entries.what: Marco and Mauro La Villa's globe-trotting documentary on the rise of the DJ from backroom technician to international star
entries.why: Q-Bert appears as himself, placing his turntablism inside the wider late-90s DJ boom that made a Q-Bert concept album commercially viable in the first place. Grade and tone diverge sharply: a conventional music documentary with interviews and club footage, sharing none of the film's animated register.

entries.title: Room 237
entries.what: Rodney Ascher's documentary in which five obsessives narrate their conflicting readings of Kubrick's The Shining, illustrated entirely with repurposed film clips
entries.why: Rodney Ascher was one of five credited editors on Wave Twisters (with Kim Bica, Syd Garon, Eric Henry and Carol Lynn Weaver) and this is his first feature as director; its method of building a film from other people's images, cut to an argument rather than a plot, comes out of the same collage instinct. Grade and tone diverge completely: Room 237 is wall-to-wall voiceover exegesis, the exact opposite of a wordless film.

entries.title: N.A.S.A.: The Spirit of Apollo
entries.what: Documentary on the making of the N.A.S.A. album, following Squeak E. Clean and DJ Zegon through sessions with George Clinton, Method Man, David Byrne and Tom Waits
entries.why: Co-directed by Syd Garon, Wave Twisters' co-director, and his only other feature as director; like Wave Twisters it takes a single record as its organising spine. Grade and tone diverge: this is a live-action studio documentary, not animation, and it talks constantly.

entries.title: Jodorowsky's Dune
entries.what: Frank Pavich's documentary on Alejandro Jodorowsky's unmade 1970s Dune, reconstructed through the storyboards of Moebius and the designs of Giger and Chris Foss
entries.why: Syd Garon did the animation on it and won the Cinema Eye Honor for Outstanding Achievement in Graphic Design or Animation for this film; the sequences that animate Moebius's boards into motion are the clearest surviving demonstration of what Garon does with still art. Grade and tone diverge: a reverent interview documentary about a psychedelic space opera rather than one you can sit inside.

entries.title: Wild Style
entries.what: Charlie Ahearn's semi-fictional Bronx film following graffiti writer Zoro, with Grandmaster Flash, Busy Bee, the Cold Crush Brothers and the Rock Steady Crew playing themselves
entries.why: The foundational film of hip-hop's four elements and the direct ancestor of Wave Twisters' premise, which is literally about rescuing graffiti, breaking, MCing and DJing from extinction; the Dental Commander, Honey Drips, Rubbish and Grandpa are one-for-one personifications of the four elements Wild Style put on screen. Grade and tone diverge: loose, sun-bleached, near-plotless naturalism rather than a cartoon at full tilt.

entries.title: Style Wars
entries.what: Tony Silver and Henry Chalfant's documentary on New York subway graffiti and the b-boys, shot as the MTA's buff campaign was destroying the work
entries.why: The canonical record of the culture as something under threat of erasure, which is exactly the stake Wave Twisters dramatises with Lord Ook's suppression of the four elements; Honey Drips the graffiti artist is unimaginable without it. Grade and tone diverge: observational documentary, and its subject is loss rather than momentum.

entries.title: Beat Street
entries.what: Stan Lathan's Bronx musical drama about an aspiring DJ, his b-boy brother and a graffiti writer, with the Rock Steady Crew, Afrika Bambaataa and Doug E. Fresh
entries.why: The studio film that fixed hip-hop's four elements as an ensemble of four character types, one per element, which is precisely the cast structure Wave Twisters uses; its DJ-as-protagonist premise is the template. Grade and tone diverge: a broad, sentimental, heavily spoken drama.

entries.title: Interstella 5555: The 5tory of the 5ecret 5tar 5ystem
entries.what: Leiji Matsumoto and Kazuhisa Takenouchi's feature-length anime with no spoken dialogue, scored end to end by Daft Punk's Discovery, in which alien musicians are abducted and rebranded as an Earth pop group
entries.why: The closest formal twin to Wave Twisters in existence: a pre-existing dance record turned into a wordless animated sci-fi feature where the music is the only narration and the images are timed to it; both even turn musicians into cartoon heroes fighting for their own art form. Tone matches as squarely as the form does.

entries.title: Fantasia
entries.what: Disney's anthology of animated sequences built around Stokowski's recordings of Bach, Dukas, Stravinsky and Mussorgsky, with no through-plot
entries.why: The origin point of the whole album-as-film idea and the only precedent Wave Twisters is routinely measured against; every choice Wave Twisters makes — pictures serving a pre-recorded score, movement cut to the beat, story kept subordinate to sound — is a turntablist answer to Fantasia's question. Grade and tone diverge: orchestral, stately, introduced by a host who explains each piece.

entries.title: Shaft
entries.what: Gordon Parks's Harlem private-eye thriller with Richard Roundtree and Isaac Hayes's wah-wah score, the film that set blaxploitation's look and sound
entries.why: Named in the Filmmaker Magazine production report as the reference for the film's Kirk-analogue, styled as an intergalactic Shaft aboard a pimped-out Enterprise; the film's entire visual wardrobe, its funk-forward soundtrack logic and its cool-hero posture are lifted from here. Note the year: 1971, not the 2000 or 2019 films of the same name. Grade and tone diverge: a slow-burn detective drama rather than a cartoon at speed.

entries.title: Bullitt
entries.what: Peter Yates's San Francisco police thriller with Steve McQueen, built around the car chase that reset the form
entries.why: The Filmmaker Magazine report states outright that a Wave Twisters chase sequence was built on a motion-reference sample from Bullitt — the animators sampled the movement the way Q-Bert samples a break. Grade and tone diverge: the chase is wordless momentum and matches, but the surrounding film is a quiet, procedural drama.

entries.title: Star Wars
entries.what: George Lucas's space opera, the serial-derived template for lasers, dogfights and a small crew against an empire
entries.why: Named in the Filmmaker Magazine report among the sci-fi classics the film riffs on; Wave Twisters' structure — a scrappy crew with one weapon against an occupying tyrant — is that template with turntables. Grade and tone diverge: dialogue-driven and paced as a three-act adventure rather than a continuous 46-minute surge.

entries.title: Star Trek: The Motion Picture
entries.what: Robert Wise's first Star Trek feature, reuniting Kirk and the Enterprise crew for a slow, effects-heavy encounter with an immense alien cloud
entries.why: The Filmmaker report names Star Trek among the sci-fi classics sampled, and Wave Twisters puts a Kirk-like figure on a pimped-out Enterprise; this is the Kirk-era feature the franchise reference resolves to, though the article names the franchise generically and the 1960s series is the likelier direct source. Grade and tone diverge hard: TMP is the most becalmed, contemplative film in this list.

entries.title: Lost in Space
entries.what: Stephen Hopkins's CGI-saturated feature revival of the Robinson family's marooned spaceship, with William Hurt and Gary Oldman
entries.why: Named in the Filmmaker report among the sci-fi staples Wave Twisters riffs on; this is the only feature the reference can point to, though the article's phrasing suggests the 1965 television series is what the animators actually had in mind. Its garish digital palette is nonetheless close to the film's video-game aesthetic.

entries.title: Godzilla
entries.what: Ishiro Honda's original kaiju film, a sombre atomic parable in which a creature woken by nuclear testing levels Tokyo
entries.why: The Filmmaker report lists Godzilla movies among the pop-culture staples the film riffs on; the monster-scale confrontations and the suit-and-miniature logic of Wave Twisters' set pieces come from this lineage. Grade and tone diverge: the 1954 original is a grief-stricken, deliberate film, nothing like the cartoon carnage it licensed.

entries.title: Yellow Submarine
entries.what: George Dunning's pop-art animated feature in which the Beatles liberate Pepperland from the music-hating Blue Meanies, built around an existing catalogue of songs
entries.why: The direct precedent for Wave Twisters' plot as well as its look: musicians as cartoon heroes restoring music to a population an antagonist has silenced, animated in flat saturated colour with sequences designed to ride each track. The psychedelic palette and gag-per-second momentum land in the same register.

entries.title: Heavy Metal
entries.what: Gerald Potterton's animated anthology of sci-fi and fantasy vignettes from the magazine, scored with Blue Oyster Cult, Black Sabbath and Devo
entries.why: The adult-animation model Wave Twisters inherits: episodic sci-fi violence in saturated airbrush colour, each sequence pinned to a rock cue, no interest in respectability or explanation. Tone is a close match for the loudness and the cartoon carnage.

entries.title: Allegro non troppo
entries.what: Bruno Bozzetto's Italian anthology setting animated sequences to Debussy, Dvorak, Ravel and Stravinsky, framed by black-and-white live-action slapstick
entries.why: The best-known irreverent answer to Fantasia, and the proof that the album-as-film form survives being made cheaply and rudely — which is the register Wave Twisters works in. Grade and tone diverge somewhat: the live-action framing is talky and the animated sections are often melancholy rather than propulsive.

entries.title: Dead Leaves
entries.what: Hiroyuki Imaishi's 52-minute Production I.G anime in which two amnesiac criminals break out of a lunar prison in a continuous escalating riot
entries.why: The nearest thing in animation to Wave Twisters' running-time-as-a-single-surge structure: roughly fifty minutes with no second act, no exposition and no let-up, drawn in flat graphic colour with the violence pitched as pure kinetic play. Tone is an exact match.

entries.title: Coonskin
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's live-action-and-animation hybrid in which Brother Rabbit, Brother Bear and Preacher Fox take over Harlem's rackets, a furious satire of American racial iconography
entries.why: The only significant animated blaxploitation feature, and the precedent for Wave Twisters doing its 1970s Black-cinema iconography in cartoon form rather than live action. Grade and tone diverge: Coonskin is verbose, bitter and deliberately ugly where Wave Twisters is playful and clean.

entries.title: Fritz the Cat
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's adaptation of Robert Crumb's strip, the first X-rated animated feature, following a college-age cat through counterculture New York
entries.why: The film that established animation as an underground medium for adults working outside the studios, which is the tradition a $250,000 self-distributed turntablist cartoon belongs to. Grade and tone diverge: Fritz is scuzzy, dialogue-heavy and slack where Wave Twisters is tight and wordless.

entries.title: Fantastic Planet
entries.what: Rene Laloux and Roland Topor's cutout-animated French-Czech feature about tiny humans kept as pets by giant blue Draags on a surreal alien world
entries.why: The standing reference point for psychedelic animated science fiction and one of the films reviewers reach for when describing Wave Twisters; the alien-biology design language and the oppressed-underclass-rebels plot are both present in the Wave Twisters cosmology. Grade and tone diverge: hypnotic and slow, with a narrator, where Wave Twisters is fast and silent.

entries.title: Space Is the Place
entries.what: John Coney's Afrofuturist feature in which Sun Ra returns from space with his Arkestra to found a Black colony on another planet, recruiting Oakland teenagers and gambling with the Overseer for the race's fate
entries.why: The same premise as Wave Twisters told in live action: a musician-hero whose instrument is literally a weapon, travelling through space to liberate his people by teaching them the music. Blaxploitation costume, cosmic sci-fi and music-as-deliverance in one film. Grade and tone diverge: loose, lo-fi and often static, with long spoken scenes.

entries.title: Superfly
entries.what: Gordon Parks Jr.'s Harlem drama about a cocaine dealer angling for one last score, carried by Curtis Mayfield's score
entries.why: Blaxploitation at the point where the soundtrack outgrew the picture and started driving it — the arrangement Wave Twisters takes to its limit by having the record come first. Its wardrobe and cool-under-pressure posture are all over Wave Twisters' character design. Grade and tone diverge: a downbeat crime drama.

entries.title: Dolemite
entries.what: D'Urville Martin's blaxploitation comedy starring Rudy Ray Moore as a pimp released from prison to clean up his club, with rhyming toasts and an all-female kung fu army
entries.why: The cheap, gleeful, deliberately absurd end of blaxploitation — rhymed boasting, martial arts and a hero whose performance style is the weapon — which is the exact tonal seam Wave Twisters mines rather than the serious end. Its toasts are also a documented ancestor of rapping. Grade and tone diverge: its comedy is verbal and its action is slack.

entries.title: Black Dynamite
entries.what: Scott Sanders's blaxploitation pastiche with Michael Jai White as an ex-CIA avenger, shot on period stock with deliberately preserved continuity errors
entries.why: The other film that reconstructs 1970s Black-action iconography from love rather than nostalgia and pushes it to cartoon extremity; it spawned an animated series for the same reason Wave Twisters skipped straight to animation. Grade and tone diverge: it is a dialogue-driven comedy whose jokes depend on you catching the reference.

entries.title: Enter the Dragon
entries.what: Robert Clouse's martial arts feature with Bruce Lee infiltrating a crime lord's island tournament, the film that broke kung fu into the West
entries.why: The source of the tournament-and-tyrant structure and of the hand-to-hand choreography Wave Twisters animates as its combat vocabulary; it is also the film that put kung fu and Black American action heroes on the same bill, a pairing the film reproduces wholesale. Grade and tone diverge: measured build-up between set pieces.

entries.title: The Wall
entries.what: Alan Parker's adaptation of the Pink Floyd album, near-dialogue-free, with Gerald Scarfe's animated sequences carrying its most extreme passages
entries.why: The best-known live-action instance of the album-as-film and one of the three titles reviewers habitually name alongside Wave Twisters; the Scarfe animation in particular does what Wave Twisters does for a whole feature — abstract imagery cut to a pre-existing record with no narration. Grade and tone diverge: grim, hostile and exhausting rather than exhilarating.

entries.title: Akira
entries.what: Katsuhiro Otomo's adaptation of his own manga, set in Neo-Tokyo where a biker's psychic powers escalate beyond containment
entries.why: The Filmmaker report names anime among the film's sources, and Akira is the specific title that taught a generation of Western animators that cel animation could be dense, kinetic and violent at feature scale; Wave Twisters' bike and vehicle sequences are drawn in its debt. Grade and tone diverge: heavily plotted and expository.

entries.title: Rock & Rule
entries.what: Clive A. Smith's Nelvana animated feature in which a rock star kidnaps a singer to summon a demon with her voice, with songs by Lou Reed, Debbie Harry, Iggy Pop and Cheap Trick
entries.why: A post-apocalyptic animated feature whose entire plot turns on music as literal power and whose set pieces are built around commissioned tracks — the same bargain Wave Twisters makes, reached from the other direction. Grade and tone diverge: it stops for dialogue scenes and its animation is conventional character work.

entries.title: Mind Game
entries.what: Masaaki Yuasa's debut feature, in which a young man shot dead in a yakuza confrontation argues his way back to life and the animation changes medium shot by shot
entries.why: The clearest demonstration that a feature can be assembled the way a DJ assembles a set — abruptly switching style and texture on the beat, trusting momentum over continuity — which is the editing grammar Wave Twisters runs on. Grade and tone diverge: it is emotionally talkative and its psychedelia serves feeling rather than spectacle.

entries.title: Breakin'
entries.what: Joel Silberg's Los Angeles dance film in which a jazz dancer falls in with two street b-boys and enters the competition circuit
entries.why: The commercial b-boy film of the moment, and the one that fixed the battle-as-narrative-climax structure Wave Twisters uses; Grandpa the breakdancer is a character type this film mass-produced. Grade and tone diverge: bright, broad and conventionally scripted.

entries.title: Krush Groove
entries.what: Michael Schultz's loosely biographical Def Jam film with Run-DMC, LL Cool J, Kurtis Blow and the Beastie Boys playing versions of themselves
entries.why: The record-label origin story of hip-hop's move from the four elements into an industry, the process Wave Twisters is implicitly protesting by treating the elements as something in need of rescue. Grade and tone diverge: an industry drama in a naturalistic register with nothing of the film's texture.

entries.title: The Freshest Kids
entries.what: Israel's documentary history of b-boying, from the Bronx through the Rock Steady Crew to the international circuit
entries.why: The definitive documentary on breaking, one of the four elements Wave Twisters personifies as Grandpa; it also reconstructs the same threatened-then-revived arc the film dramatises. Grade and tone diverge: standard archive-and-interview documentary construction.

entries.title: Copyright Criminals
entries.what: Benjamin Franzen and Kembrew McLeod's documentary on sampling and the law, with Public Enemy, De La Soul, Clyde Stubblefield and Steve Albini
entries.why: The argument underneath Wave Twisters made explicit: a record built from other people's records as a legitimate act of authorship. Wave Twisters is the same claim made in pictures, assembling itself from NASA imagery and old cartoons. Grade and tone diverge: an issue documentary with lawyers and talking heads.

entries.title: Kung Fu Hustle
entries.what: Stephen Chow's martial arts comedy in which a slum tenement's hidden masters defend it against the Axe Gang, with physics borrowed openly from Looney Tunes
entries.why: Live action filmed as if it were a cartoon: impossible impacts, chase geometry that ignores space, jokes delivered entirely through movement. Tone is a strong match — the same delight in stylised violence at speed — while the actual connection is only a shared debt to kung fu cinema and cartoon physics.

entries.title: Redline
entries.what: Takeshi Koike's Madhouse anime about an illegal interplanetary race, hand-drawn across roughly a hundred thousand cels
entries.why: Tone is an unusually close match: relentless forward motion, thick graphic linework, deafening sound design and a plot that exists only to justify the next sequence. The connection itself is only shared sensibility — no documented link to Wave Twisters, which is why the grade sits low against the tone.

entries.title: Kung Fury
entries.what: David Sandberg's 31-minute crowdfunded pastiche in which a Miami cop time-travels to kill Hitler, built from VHS-artefact digital compositing and a synthwave score
entries.why: The nearest modern equivalent to Wave Twisters' bargain: a half-hour independently financed genre-worship film, entirely composited on a desktop, carried by a record and never once stopping to explain itself. Tone is a direct match; the connection is purely one of method and attitude, hence the low grade. Marked as a short.

entries.title: Fantasia 2000
entries.what: Disney's sequel anthology of animated sequences set to Beethoven, Gershwin, Shostakovich and Stravinsky, mixing hand-drawn work with early CGI
entries.why: The contemporary of Wave Twisters in the same form, released while Wave Twisters was in production, and a useful contrast: the same music-first structure executed with a studio budget and celebrity introductions. Its Rhapsody in Blue segment is the closest a Disney film gets to the flat graphic city-cartoon look.

entries.title: Sita Sings the Blues
entries.what: Nina Paley's solo-made animated feature retelling the Ramayana through 1920s Annette Hanshaw recordings, animated largely in Flash
entries.why: A feature animated by essentially one person on a desktop, structured around pre-existing recordings and then given away free — the same independent-production and self-distribution logic Q-Bert used when he put Wave Twisters out on unprotected home video. Its copyright fight is the sampling argument again.

entries.title: American Pop
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's rotoscoped generational saga following one immigrant family through a century of American popular music
entries.why: An animated feature whose structure is dictated by a soundtrack of existing records, each era's song setting the visual style of its section; it is the music-history-as-animation experiment Wave Twisters narrows to a single genre.

entries.title: The Point!
entries.what: Fred Wolf's animated feature built from Harry Nilsson's concept album, about a round-headed boy banished from a land where everything is pointed
entries.why: An early and near-forgotten instance of the same manoeuvre: a musician's concept album animated into a feature, with the record supplying both structure and moral. Its outcast-hero parable is the same shape as Wave Twisters' four-elements rescue.

entries.title: Heavy Traffic
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's part-animated, part-live-action portrait of a cartoonist's New York, assembled from photographs, pinball imagery and cel work
entries.why: Bakshi's most formally restless film and the clearest precedent for cutting animation against photographic and found material in a jagged, collage-like way — the assembly method the Wave Twisters team described as putting sources together scratchlike.

entries.title: Wizards
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's post-apocalyptic fantasy in which two wizard brothers fight over a recovered film projector used as a propaganda weapon
entries.why: A cheaply made animated feature whose plot turns on control of a recovered media technology — the same device as the Wave Twister wristwatch turntable — and which resorts to rotoscoped stock footage and cut-out collage whenever the budget runs out, as Wave Twisters resorts to NASA stills.

entries.title: Belladonna of Sadness
entries.what: Eiichi Yamamoto's Mushi Production feature, largely held on watercolour and ink panels panned by the camera, scored with psychedelic rock and jazz
entries.why: The far end of what animation can do with limited motion and a strong score: still images carried entirely by music and camera movement, which is the economy Wave Twisters works within. Grade and tone diverge somewhat: it is slow, erotic and desolate rather than propulsive.

entries.title: Robot Carnival
entries.what: Nine-segment anime anthology from Katsuhiro Otomo, Koji Morimoto, Yasuomi Umetsu and others, with most segments carrying no dialogue at all
entries.why: An anthology that proves at feature length how far animation travels on music and movement alone, with Joe Hisaishi's score doing the work dialogue would otherwise do; its opening and closing sequences are the purest wordless spectacle in commercial anime.

entries.title: Tekkonkinkreet
entries.what: Michael Arias's anime about two street kids defending Treasure Town from developers and yakuza, in Taiyo Matsumoto's warped graffiti-dense cityscapes
entries.why: The best animated rendering of a city as a surface written on by its inhabitants, which is what Honey Drips's graffiti stands for in Wave Twisters; its gravity-indifferent rooftop chases are the same kinetic idiom.

entries.title: Ninja Scroll
entries.what: Yoshiaki Kawajiri's anime about a wandering swordsman fighting eight demon assassins, each with a grotesque supernatural ability
entries.why: The template for the animated duel against a sequence of themed monsters, which is exactly how Wave Twisters structures its second half; both films treat each opponent as an excuse for a new visual idea rather than a plot development.

entries.title: Cool World
entries.what: Ralph Bakshi's live-action and animation hybrid in which a cartoonist is pulled into the lurid city his own drawings inhabit
entries.why: The nearest thing to Wave Twisters' clash of registers — flat cartoon figures moving through garish rendered space at cartoon-physics speed — and, like it, a film whose design work considerably outruns its story.

entries.title: Five Deadly Venoms
entries.what: Chang Cheh's Shaw Brothers film in which five graduates of a kung fu school, each trained in one of five venomous-creature styles — centipede, snake, scorpion, lizard, toad — are hunted down by their junior
entries.why: The specific martial arts film whose five named, single-power fighters became hip-hop's favourite structural borrowing; Wave Twisters' roster of one-gimmick characters facing a tyrant's themed minions is that pattern, and it is the same Shaw Brothers vocabulary the Wu-Tang generation sampled.

entries.title: Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song
entries.what: Melvin Van Peebles's independently made, independently distributed film about a sex-show performer on the run after beating two policemen, scored by Earth, Wind & Fire
entries.why: The founding independent Black feature, largely wordless for long stretches, driven by its funk score and psychedelic superimposition, and self-distributed outside the studios — the same route Q-Bert took with Wave Twisters. The film that made Shaft and everything after it possible.

entries.title: The Last Angel of History
entries.what: John Akomfrah's essay film on Afrofuturism, threading Sun Ra, George Clinton, Derrick May and DJ Spooky through the figure of a data thief searching for the black secret technology
entries.why: The intellectual frame Wave Twisters sits inside without knowing it: Black musicians reimagined as space travellers and the turntable treated as alien technology. It names the tradition the film is an artefact of. Grade and tone diverge: a slow, dense, heavily narrated essay.

entries.title: Sample This
entries.what: Dan Forrer's documentary tracing how the Incredible Bongo Band's Apache became the break that hip-hop was built on
entries.why: A single-record history of the raw material turntablists work with; it explains, in the only way a documentary can, why a Q-Bert record is a record made of other records. Grade and tone diverge: a narrated archival documentary.

entries.title: Bomb It
entries.what: Jon Reiss's documentary following graffiti and street artists across five continents, from Taki 183 to Sao Paulo pixadores
entries.why: The global continuation of the graffiti element Honey Drips represents, and a record of the same criminalisation-and-survival dynamic Wave Twisters casts as Lord Ook's suppression. Grade and tone diverge: an interview documentary with no visual kinship to the film.

entries.title: Infamy
entries.what: Doug Pray's documentary on six graffiti writers and the man who cleans their work off, shot as a set of character studies
entries.why: Made by Doug Pray immediately after Scratch, extending his DJ film into the neighbouring element; between them the two cover half of Wave Twisters' four. Grade and tone diverge: quiet, observational and character-driven.

entries.title: Waking Life
entries.what: Richard Linklater's rotoscoped feature in which a dreamer drifts between monologues on free will, consciousness and cinema, each segment animated by a different artist
entries.why: The other American independent animated feature of 2001 made on desktop software by a distributed team of artists, each bringing an incompatible style; the production model and the festival-circuit route are the same as Wave Twisters'. Grade and tone diverge completely: it is nothing but talk.

entries.title: Daft Punk's Electroma
entries.what: Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo's live-action feature following two helmeted robots through the American desert, with no dialogue and no Daft Punk music
entries.why: A musician-directed, entirely wordless feature by the act behind Interstella 5555, which makes it the useful negative case for the form: proof that removing dialogue guarantees nothing about pace. Grade and tone diverge as far as they can — it is glacial and austere where Wave Twisters is relentless.

entries.title: Son of the White Mare
entries.what: Marcell Jankovics's Hungarian feature from the Feherlofia legend: three brothers born of a white mare descend into the underworld to fight dragons, animated in flat fields of hot colour that transform continuously
entries.why: The most spectacular version of what Wave Twisters is doing: a quest told almost entirely through graphic transformation, where shapes become other shapes on the beat and colour does the work a plot would otherwise have to. It belongs beside the key's Fantastic Planet and Belladonna of Sadness, and is arguably the better pick of the three for this film's whirl of morphing forms. Jankovics is mythic and solemn where Q-Bert's film is a cartoon with jokes in it.

entries.title: Street of Crocodiles
entries.what: The Quay Brothers' twenty-one-minute stop-motion short after Bruno Schulz: a puppet is released into a decaying arcade of screws, dust and tailors' dummies, scored by Lech Jankowski
entries.why: Defensible only as wordless animation carried by its score, with no dialogue and nothing explained, which is a real formal kinship and plainly the reason it was suggested. But the pleasures do not transfer. The Quays work in sepia decay, dust and dread at short-film scale, and Wave Twisters is flat, bright, funky and comic, made for an audience that came for turntablism. This one looked strong on sight and does not hold up on inspection.

entries.title: Paprika
entries.what: Satoshi Kon's final feature: a device that lets therapists enter their patients' dreams is stolen, and a parade of appliances and dolls floods waking Tokyo
entries.why: The same structure, a chase through worlds that reorganise themselves every few minutes, where transitions happen on a musical cue and no rule is ever explained. Kon cuts to Hirasawa's score the way Wave Twisters cuts to Q-Bert's, so the track drives the montage instead of accompanying it, and the film sits beside the key's Mind Game. Kon is technically immaculate and psychologically serious, where Wave Twisters is a scratch record with drawings on it.

entries.title: Aeon Flux
entries.what: Peter Chung's animated shorts for MTV's Liquid Television, a six-part serial in 1991 followed by five shorts in 1992 and a half-hour series in 1995, in which a leather-clad assassin dies at the end of almost every episode. This entry rates the original animation, not the 2005 live-action feature of the same name
entries.why: Chung's shorts are effectively without speech, which is Wave Twisters' single most distinctive quality: a story told entirely through movement, design and sound with no dialogue to lean on. Both come out of the same MTV-era underground animation culture and share its taste for elongated stylised bodies, violence choreographed as dance, and invention offered without explanation. It is marked as a series rather than a film, which bears on which catalogue it resolves against and not at all on how good a watch-next it is. Chung's sleek, erotic dystopia is a colder register than Q-Bert's funk cartoon.

entries.title: The Thief and the Cobbler
entries.what: Richard Williams's animated feature, in production from 1964 and taken out of his hands in 1992: a near-silent cobbler and a thief blunder through a Golden City of impossible geometric perspective. Indexed at 1993, the year of the Allied Filmmakers cut; Williams's own ninety-one-minute workprint dates from 1992
entries.why: Two near-wordless protagonists whose entire characterisation is movement, in a film where the animation is the attraction and the plot is a frame on which to hang set pieces, which is exactly how Wave Twisters is built. Both are also obsessive independent features made outside the studio system by people who would not stop, and both survive in versions their authors had to fight for. Sits with the key's Rock & Rule at grade 2. Williams's ornate Islamic geometry is a world away from the film's urban funk.

entries.title: The Iron Giant
entries.what: Brad Bird's hand-drawn feature: a boy in 1957 Maine hides a fifty-foot alien machine from the Army while it decides not to be a weapon
entries.why: Shares the word 'animation' with the target and nothing else. It is a warm, classically constructed, heavily scripted children's film whose whole effect depends on dialogue and on a sacrifice you are meant to cry at; Wave Twisters is a forty-six-minute wordless scratch record with pictures, in which a dentist-astronaut fights a tyrant to recover breakdancing. This is the head of a run of nine consecutive titles beginning with 'The' that one model produced for this target, and it is a fair sample of the rest.

entries.title: The City of Lost Children
entries.what: Jeunet and Caro's designed dystopia: a fairground strongman searches for his stolen brother in a port city where a scientist harvests children's dreams
entries.why: The previous pass rated this against three other targets and found it defensible only once, on a shared appetite for invented worlds. That much is present here too — a gallery of grotesques, a tyrant who steals something vital from the young, a milieu fabricated down to the rivets. It does not reach a grade because everything the target's viewer came for is absent: live action, densely talky, sepia and cluttered, cut for atmosphere rather than to a beat, with no music-first structure at all. Wave Twisters is flat, bright, silent and pinned to a record.

entries.title: The Secret of Kells
entries.what: Tomm Moore and Nora Twomey's Irish feature: a boy in the abbey of Kells is drawn into the forest by the spirit Aisling and into finishing an illuminated manuscript, animated in flattened Insular-art perspective
entries.why: Defensible on design. Kells is one of very few features that subordinates volume, depth and camera to flat pattern and colour, taking its entire visual grammar from an existing graphic tradition rather than from photography — the same bargain Wave Twisters makes with graffiti and airbrushed sleeve art. The key holds Son of the White Mare for a more spectacular version of that argument and Tekkonkinkreet for the city-as-surface version, and Kells adds less than either. It is also lyrical, gentle, dialogue-driven and made for children, where the target is loud, comic and nailed to a scratch record.

entries.title: The Red Balloon
entries.what: Albert Lamorisse's thirty-four-minute short: a boy in Ménilmontant is followed through the streets by a balloon with a will of its own, until other children destroy it. Marked as a short
entries.why: One thing carries, and only one: it is a wordless film of comparable length driven entirely by movement and a score, and wordlessness is the target's defining formal fact, so the pairing is not nothing. That is the end of the case. Lamorisse is photographing a real boy in real Paris streets and building a gentle parable about persecution and grace; Wave Twisters is drawn, and its pleasures are cartoon violence, blaxploitation costume and turntable gags at speed. The previous pass gave Street of Crocodiles a grade 1 on this same formal ground, and Street of Crocodiles has more to offer, because it is at least animation.

entries.title: The Secret of Roan Inish
entries.what: John Sayles's live-action film: a girl sent to her grandparents on the Donegal coast pieces together the family story of a selkie and a lost brother
entries.why: No connection of any kind. A quiet naturalistic live-action folk tale about family memory, recommended to a hip-hop concept album animated as a cartoon. It is the third of four consecutive 'The Secret' titles this model produced for this target — Kells, Roan Inish, NIMH, Garden — which is the clearest single piece of evidence in the pool that it was generating title-shaped strings rather than recommending films.

entries.title: The Princess and the Warrior
entries.what: Tom Tykwer's German film, Der Krieger und die Kaiserin: a psychiatric nurse whose life is saved by a drifter under a lorry pursues him into his life and his brother's bank robbery. The year in the suggestion, 2009, is wrong — the film premiered at Venice on 2 September 2000 and opened in Germany that October
entries.why: Nothing in this film touches the target. It is a slow, sombre live-action romance about damage, and its most famous sequence is a tracheotomy performed under a truck. If the association was Tykwer's reputation for cutting to music, the film to reach for would have been Run Lola Run, and even that would only have been a grade 1 on kinetic editing. A wrong year on top of a wrong film.

entries.title: The Secret of NIMH
entries.what: Don Bluth's first feature after walking out of Disney: a field mouse seeks help from a colony of laboratory-enhanced rats to move her house before the plough reaches it
entries.why: Traditional full animation at its most classically rendered — volumetric, atmospheric, backlit, and entirely dialogue-driven — which is the precise opposite of what Wave Twisters does with flat graphic figures on a beat. The one parallel available, that Bluth left a studio to make the film he wanted, is a production anecdote; the key already covers independent animation properly with Sita Sings the Blues, The Thief and the Cobbler and the Bakshi titles, each of which shares something visible with the target as well.

entries.title: The Last Unicorn
entries.what: Rankin/Bass's animated feature, drawn by Topcraft from Peter S. Beagle's novel: a unicorn travels to find the rest of her kind, taken by the Red Bull
entries.why: A gentle, mournful, heavily scored fantasy with a great deal of dialogue and a literary source, and no point of contact with a forty-six-minute wordless turntablist cartoon. Recommended on 'mythic, poetic, and richly atmospheric' — adjectives this same model attached, almost verbatim, to three of its other suggestions for this target, which is what that phrasing is for.

entries.title: The Secret Garden
entries.what: Agnieszka Holland's live-action adaptation of the Burnett novel: an orphaned girl sent to a Yorkshire house finds a walled garden and the invalid cousin nobody mentions
entries.why: Live action, period, English, literary, and about the recovery of feeling in children. No animation, no music-led structure, no wordlessness, no hip-hop, no kinetics, nothing. The fourth title in the 'The Secret' run, and the point at which the pattern stops being arguable as coincidence.

entries.title: Koyaanisqatsi
entries.what: Godfrey Reggio's non-narrative feature, photographed by Ron Fricke and scored by Philip Glass: time-lapse and slow-motion images of landscape, industry and cities, with no dialogue, no characters and no commentary
entries.why: The purest instance in cinema of the thing the target is doing — picture and score built as a single object, the cut determined by the music, and nothing whatever explained — and it is absent from the key, which reaches for Fantasia and The Wall on this axis. Its accelerated city passages, where traffic, escalators and assembly lines are cut into pulses against Glass's arpeggios, are the closest a feature comes to Wave Twisters' habit of letting a rhythm decide what the eye gets next. Reggio is solemn and awed where Q-Bert's film is funky and comic, and it has no characters at all, which caps the tone.

entries.title: Pi
entries.what: Darren Aronofsky's debut in grainy high-contrast black-and-white: a number theorist in a Chinatown flat hunts a 216-digit pattern he believes governs the markets and the Torah, scored by Clint Mansell with Aphex Twin, Autechre and Massive Attack
entries.why: Defensible on the cut. Aronofsky's ritual montages — pills, headphones, needle, pupil — are assembled exactly the way a DJ assembles a bar, short identical units repeated and varied against an electronic pulse, and the film's energy is entirely a function of its record. Both are also films made for almost nothing by people who could afford rhythm and not much else. What it does not share is everything on the surface: monochrome paranoia inside one man's skull, live action, no jokes, no crowd, no colour. The title already sits in the American Astronaut and Avalon keys on different arguments, and is judged here on its own.

entries.title: Cat Soup
entries.what: Tatsuo Sato's thirty-four-minute anime from Nekojiru's manga: a kitten follows his sister's divided soul through a sequence of surreal cruelties — a dismembering magician, a drowned world, a god who switches off time — with no dialogue at all. Marked as a short
entries.why: Released the same year, at two-thirds the running time, and wordless end to end: a story told purely through drawn movement and a score, in episodes that transform without warning and are never explained. That is Wave Twisters' construction exactly, and it sits with the key's Dead Leaves as the other short-form anime that runs on invention rather than plot, with grotesque violence played as play. Sato's register is sweet-sour and finally sad, with cruelty that lands, where the target is triumphant and funny, so the tone parts even where the form does not.

entries.title: The Spine of Night
entries.what: Philip Gelatt and Morgan Galen King's rotoscoped adult fantasy, hand-drawn over live-action footage at twelve frames a second across seven years of animation: a magical bloom passes from hand to hand over centuries, corrupting a scholar, then a tyrant, then everyone who reaches for it, with Richard E. Grant, Lucy Lawless and Patton Oswalt on the voice track
entries.why: Defensible on the settled ground that an obsessive, unusual piece of independent animation is a real recommendation here whatever it is about, and this one has the pedigree to go with it: Gelatt and King name Frazetta and Bakshi's Fire and Ice, which puts it directly downstream of the Heavy Metal and Bakshi titles the key already carries. What it does not inherit is why those titles rate as highly as they do. Heavy Metal is a 2 on tone because it is episodic, funny and cut to a record; The Spine of Night is humourless, doom-laden and carried by narration and dialogue, ninety-three minutes of arterial gore in a muted palette. The target is forty-six wordless minutes of flat, bright, funky cartoon pinned to a scratch record, and there is nothing in this film that feels like sitting through that.

entries.title: Liquid Television
entries.what: MTV's animation showcase, produced by Colossal Pictures with a Mark Mothersbaugh theme and running four seasons and twenty-seven episodes from 2 June 1991 to January 1995: half-hour blocks of shorts from underground cartoonists and the Spike and Mike festival circuit, and the show that launched Aeon Flux and Beavis and Butt-Head
entries.why: This is the culture Wave Twisters came out of, and the key already holds a piece of it - Aeon Flux, rated at 2, was a Liquid Television serial. The parent gives you the whole of what that entry gives you and more of it: segment after segment of flat graphic design, elongated stylised bodies, cartoon violence as choreography, and invention handed over with no explanation and frequently no dialogue, cut at the pace of a mixtape by people whose reference was record sleeves and skate graphics rather than studio animation. Tone is a 2 because the experience genuinely rhymes - thirty minutes of wordless graphic ideas at speed with jokes in them is close to the forty-six minutes the target offers. The honest deductions are that it is an anthology, so the register wanders and some segments are talky, and that there is no turntablism and no hip-hop anywhere in it, which is why it is not a 3 alongside Scratch and Wild Style.

entries.title: Street Trash
entries.what: J. Michael Muro's hundred-thousand-dollar Brooklyn splatter comedy: a liquor store owner sells a crate of prohibition-era Tenafly Viper to the derelicts of a Greenpoint junkyard and they dissolve into coloured fluid, while a gang led by a deranged veteran and a cop investigating the deaths fill out the rest of the 101 minutes
entries.why: Nothing carries. No animation, no wordlessness, no music-led cutting, no graphic design, no hip-hop - a live-action, dialogue-driven, deliberately offensive melt movie whose producer said he wrote it to offend every group on the planet. The one thread available to pull, that bodies deform in lurid colour like cartoon bodies, is a latex effect rather than a graphic idea, and the key already covers grotesque violence played as play with Dead Leaves and Cat Soup, both of which are drawn, wordless and cut to a score. What is left is the shelf: low-budget, urban, 1980s, cult. Wild Style and Beat Street are on that shelf and rate 3 for reasons that actually touch the target, and this film is on it for none of them.

entries.title: Mad God
entries.what: Phil Tippett's stop-motion feature, assembled intermittently across some thirty years: a figure descends by diving bell through strata of a ruined industrial hell, past surgeries, furnaces and armies of shambling drones, with no dialogue at all
entries.why: Defensible on the settled ground, which is that an obsessive, unusual, handmade piece of animation is a real answer for this target whatever its subject — the key admits Aeon Flux, Son of the White Mare and The Thief and the Cobbler on exactly that. Mad God has the strongest version of the production claim on the list: one animator, no system, decades of unpaid time, every frame built by hand, and a feature that exists only because he would not stop, which is the bargain a self-distributed quarter-million-dollar turntablist cartoon made on a smaller scale. It is also wordless from end to end, the target's single most distinctive formal fact, and it is built the way the key rewards in Ninja Scroll: a descent through set pieces, each an excuse for a new visual idea rather than a plot development, none of them explained. What caps the grade is the thing that actually defines Wave Twisters, which is that a record came first and the pictures are timed to it. Nothing in Mad God is pinned to a beat; Dan Wool's score follows the images rather than driving them, and there is no music-first structure to speak of. Tone holds at 1 only because of the wordlessness — the key put The Spine of Night at 0 for being carried by narration, and this is not — and everything else parts: brown, wet, fetid and dreadful, with cruelty that lands, against forty-six minutes of flat bright funk with jokes in it that ends in triumph.

entries.title: Rocks in My Pockets
entries.what: Signe Baumane's Latvian-American animated feature: the director narrates her own family's history of depression and suicide through five women across a century, with hand-drawn figures composited over twenty-eight physical sets she built and photographed, and some thirty thousand drawings behind it
entries.why: The mode is the case and the mode is the whole of it. This is a feature animated essentially by one person over years, funded on grants and a Kickstarter and then toured by its own director, which is the independent-production and self-distribution logic the key holds Sita Sings the Blues at grade 1 for, and Baumane's hybrid of drawn bodies moving over hand-built papier-mache sets is genuinely inventive craft of the kind this key has already agreed is worth something on its own. It goes no higher because it is the target's opposite on the axis that matters most. Wave Twisters is wordless for forty-six minutes and its entire construction is pictures cut to a record; Rocks in My Pockets is eighty-eight minutes of continuous first-person narration in the director's own voice, a rueful literary monologue about depression in which the pictures illustrate the talk. The key put Waking Life at tone 0 for precisely this, the other independent desktop animation of its moment and nothing but talk, and this is that entry again with a smaller crew and a heavier subject.
